selected_news.summary: Athens Registered Latest Objections to Turkey-Libya Deal on UN Record tovima.com
selected_news.source_headline: tovima.com - Breaking News, Analysis and Opinion from To Vima’s International Edition
selected_news.article_text: Greece has formally reiterated its objections to the 2019 Turkey-Libya maritime agreement in a letter to United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres, following its approval by Libya’s eastern-based House of Representatives last month The letter, sent on October 22 by Greece’s Permanent Representative to the UN, Ambassador Aglaia Balta, on instructions from Foreign Minister George Gerapetritis, was subsequently circulated as an official UN General Assembly document under the heading of the law of the sea (A/81/455) Athens maintains that the memorandum, which seeks to delimit maritime jurisdiction areas between Turkey and Libya in the eastern Mediterranean, is incompatible with international law and cannot produce legal effects for third countries The Greek position is that Turkey and Libya do not have opposite or adjacent coastlines that would provide a legal basis for the delimitation, while the agreement disregards the maritime entitlements of Greek islands, particularly Crete and the Dodecanese NEWSLETTER TABLE TALK The circulation of the letter formally places Greece’s objections on the UN record but does not constitute a UN ruling on the agreement or an endorsement of Athens’ legal arguments The Greek diplomatic initiative follows the October 20 decision by Libya’s eastern-based House of Representatives to approve the 2019 memorandum, reversing its previous opposition to the agreement The memorandum was originally signed in November 2019 between Turkey and Libya’s then internationally recognized Government of National Accord, based in Tripoli. The eastern-based parliament, aligned with military commander Khalifa Haftar, had rejected the agreement and withheld its approval for years The October vote also reversed earlier parliamentary decisions to reject agreements with Turkey and sever political ties with Ankara The decision drew strong reactions from Greece, Egypt and Cyprus, all of which consider the agreement detrimental to their maritime claims in the region Turkey welcomed the Libyan parliament’s approval, maintaining that the agreement safeguards the mutual rights and interests of the two countries under international law Athens, by contrast, reiterated that the parliamentary decision does not change the memorandum’s legal status and cannot override the rights of other coastal states The European Union also rejected the agreement. EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said the bloc considered the memorandum incompatible with the law of the sea, infringing upon the sovereign rights of third countries and incapable of producing legal consequences for them European Council President António Costa and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen similarly reiterated the EU’s position following the Libyan vote Tourism growth is expected to continue in 2027 with UK airlines planning to expand seating capacity to Greece

Mektup, Yunanistan'ın Daimi Temsilcisi Aglaia Balta tarafından, Dışişleri Bakanı George Gerapetritis'in talimatıyla hazırlandı. selected_news.summary: Minister hints at restriction on selling technology ‘to certain users’ amid worries over surreptitious filming of women The government is considering placing restrictions on smart glasses amid concerns the technology is being used to surreptitiously film women, a minister has said. Speaking in the House of Commons, the safeguarding minister, Satvir Kaur, hinted at a ban on selling the technology “to certain users”. Continue reading...
selected_news.source_headline: UK government considers smart glasses ban over secret filming concerns
selected_news.article_text: Minister hints at restriction on selling technology ‘to certain users’ amid worries over surreptitious filming of women The government is considering placing restrictions on smart glasses amid concerns the technology is being used to surreptitiously film women, a minister has said Speaking in the House of Commons, the safeguarding minister, Satvir Kaur, hinted at a ban on selling the technology “to certain users” Kaur said: “The benefits of smart glasses must be weighed against the harms they can cause. The government is already looking into options to restrict smart glasses in certain settings and restricting the sale to certain users.” The minister said people who used smart glasses for filming already risked breaking the law in certain settings, such as in a court where cameras are prohibited Kaur added: “Other settings, such as healthcare and education, have existing safeguarding or professional policies that are relevant to smart glasses and any kind of digital recording. NHS England and the Department for Education are currently looking into wearable technology in certain settings as well.” Anna Sabine, a Liberal Democrat MP and a culture spokesperson for the party who held Wednesday’s debate, said: “Women are reporting waking up after nights out to find videos of themselves have gone viral online, filmed without their knowledge or consent by men wearing smart glasses “To me, these devices not only have the potential to erode safety and privacy in public spaces, but raise really important questions about consent.” She said one of the selling points of the glasses in advertisements was that they could be used “to film discreetly”. Sabine said she did not want parliamentarians to “only regulate once it is too late” Kaur said smart glasses, which can come with built-in cameras, microphones and displays, could “be hugely beneficial” to some people. “For example, for those that are visually impaired, smart glasses have been a gamechanger, helping them navigate the world around them.” A politician in the Senedd has defended his use of smart glasses in the debating chamber. Jason O’Connell, a Reform UK MS for Pontypridd Cynon Merthyr, read a speech from an in-built teleprompter feature in his glasses last month He told the BBC’s Politics Wales: “One of the things I identified, a weakness of mine, was that my head was down looking at my notes a lot and I wanted to get away from that.”

selected_news.title: Burnham, Karayiplere 40 Milyon £'luk Altyapı Paketi Açtı
selected_news.summary: Leading figures in Caribbean reparatory justice movement speak out after UK PM announced infrastructure package Offers of debt relief and development assistance from the UK cannot be a replacement for reparations for centuries of slavery, leading figures in the Caribbean reparatory justice movement have said. Their comments follow British prime minister Andy Burnham’s announcement on Friday that he wanted to begin a structured dialogue on slavery and reparations and was open to Britain apologising , but ruled out reparations. Continue reading...
selected_news.source_headline: Debt relief and aid no replacement for slavery reparations, UK told
selected_news.article_text: Leading figures in Caribbean reparatory justice movement speak out after UK PM announced infrastructure package Offers of debt relief and development assistance from the UK cannot be a replacement for reparations for centuries of slavery, leading figures in the Caribbean reparatory justice movement have said Their comments follow British prime minister Andy Burnham’s announcement on Friday that he wanted to begin a structured dialogue on slavery and reparations and was open to Britain apologising, but ruled out reparations Instead, he proposed discussions on debt resets for smaller Commonwealth nations and announced £40m ($54m) for critical infrastructure in the Caribbean over the next three years As leaders of the 56-member Commonwealth bloc meet in a private retreat at their summit in Antigua, Ralph Gonsalves, a former prime minister of St Vincent and the Grenadines and a senior figure in the reparatory justice movement’s Repair Campaign, said that while countries in the region were likely to welcome Burnham’s offer, the Caribbean would resist any attempt to treat debt restructuring or development assistance as a form of reparation A 10-point plan drawn up by the Caribbean Community’s reparations commission, which outlines the region’s vision for reparations, specifically asks for “debt cancellation”– not debt restructuring – and “monetary compensation”, arguing that former colonies’ “existing debts are intergenerational and are ultimately and intimately tied to centuries of colonial extraction” “When I listened to Andy Burnham, and I listened to the king, and they’re talking about what is helpful is not reparations, but for them to work on specific things like debt relief, and education and health, and climate change infrastructure “Now, all those things are within the 10-point plan. But they are also within the sustainable development goals of 2015, which we all signed on to at the United Nations,” he told the Guardian He added: “There are things in the reparatory justice 10-point plan which deal with issues … the first one is the ecology, and then psychological repair. And for people like members of the Rastafari faith, or brothers and sisters who may wish repatriation, that’s something we have to work out with African countries, those who want to go back. But there are financial implications in that. So you’ll have to have a separate carve-out on the basis of the 10-point plan.” Labour MP Bell Ribeiro-Addy, chair of the House of Commons’ all-party parliamentary group for Afrikan Reparations, said the question was fundamentally about “agency” Speaking at an event on Tuesday to launch a global reparations caravan, which will travel across countries to educate and engage people in the reparations movement, she said: “So when it comes now to reparative justice, and as we move forward in the movement, I have to be clear with everybody, it has to be about agency, not making deals here and there, because agency was the crime. When you think about what was taken from people of African descent when they were enslaved, it was their agency, their right to decide all of these different things about their lives “So when reparative justice arrangements are being made, it absolutely has to be made with those who were affected, because if it is done to us, it is not reparations. I don’t know what it is, but it is not reparative justice.” Gonsalves said the danger of reducing reparatory justice to development assistance was that such assistance remained discretionary on the UK’s part. “We have to understand the specificities of reparatory justice as distinct from general sustainable development goals. They’re shaping the discussion only within the frame of sustainable development goals,” he said Prof Kingsley Abbott, a human rights lawyer and director of the Institute of Commonwealth Studies at the University of London, also stressed the importance of harmed communities having a decisive say in what reparations should entail Speaking at the global reparations caravan launch on Tuesday, he said: “It’s for you to say. It’s your story. It’s your lived experience. But it’s time to start listening to those who continue to suffer from those crimes even today. It’s time to listen to you and to listen and learn from you “I reflected on my work as a human rights lawyer in different parts of the world. And in that time, I’ve met with many different victims of serious human rights violations, atrocity crimes, and their families and their descendants in places like Guatemala, Colombia, Nepal, Myanmar. And here in Antigua tonight, I’m meeting with all of you “Wherever those victims of those terrible crimes and their families were from, and whatever their faith, whatever their ethnicity, whatever their beliefs, they all had one thing in common. When I met with them, they all said that they wanted justice. And they wanted not only justice, but they wanted to be made whole again.” A spokesperson for the Foreign Office said: “The prime minister wants to build stronger relationships to renew the relevance of the Commonwealth in a new era. We will do that by facing our past together and focusing on a future where every person living within it has equality, security and hope “We are already committed to working with Commonwealth partners on issues facing the world, including the role of private finance in tackling global debt issues, addressing the climate crisis, and supporting economic development. We will continue to do so.”
